title: Test your S3 data lake basics
guideLabel: Re-read what a lake is made of

questions.q: A teammate says, 'We have an S3 bucket, so we have a data lake.' What is the fairest reply?
options: Yes, an S3 bucket and a data lake are the same thing
Only if the bucket holds more than 1 TB
S3 is the storage layer, and a lake also needs a way to organise and query the files
No, a data lake can never use S3
questions.explain: S3 stores files. A data lake adds the pieces that make those files usable: a table format, a catalog that lists the tables, and an engine that runs queries.

questions.q: Why can a plain pile of Parquet files in S3 be awkward when many jobs change data at once?
options: Parquet files cannot be read by SQL tools
S3 has no all-or-nothing update across many files
S3 only allows one file per bucket
questions.explain: S3 keeps each single file update atomic, but there is no atomic update across several files. A table format such as Apache Iceberg adds that missing layer.

questions.q: Which job does the Glue Data Catalog do in an S3 data lake?
options: It stores the data files themselves
It lists the tables and where their files live
It speeds up the network between S3 and your laptop
It deletes old files for you
questions.explain: Think of the catalog as the index at the back of a book. The files stay in S3, and the catalog tells query tools which tables exist and where to find them.

questions.q: A query tool bills by data scanned. Which change usually lowers the bill most?
options: Storing the same data as one big text file
Storing it in a columnar format such as Parquet
questions.explain: Columnar files let the engine skip columns the query does not ask for. That means fewer bytes scanned, and so a smaller bill.
